opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that on a GPU, the fundamental execution model is kernel by kernel. You take your model, you break it into a sequence of kernels, and each kernel runs across the whole machine. So you launch a kernel, it reads its inputs from high-bandwidth memory, does its compute, writes its results back out to HBM, and then the next kernel starts. In a sense the operations are serialized in time. And the way you get efficiency in that model is with batch: you make the batch big enough that each kernel has enough parallelism to fill all those streaming multiprocessors, and enough reuse that you amortize the cost of going back and forth to memory and the kernel launch overhead.

On the RDU, which is the Reconfigurable Dataflow Unit we build at SambaNova, the model is different. Instead of serializing the operations in time, we lay them out in space. You take a big chunk of the dataflow graph, potentially many layers, and map it onto the chip so that different operators are running on different parts of the hardware at the same time, and the data streams from one operator to the next through on-chip memory and the interconnect. So it's a pipeline. You're getting parallelism not just within an operator but across operators, and you're not bouncing intermediate results back to off-chip memory between every step.

What that means for batch is that you don't need nearly as large a batch to get high utilization. On the GPU, small batch means each kernel is starved: you can't fill the machine, and you're memory-bandwidth bound. On the RDU, because you've got this pipeline of operators all running concurrently, even a small batch, or individual samples, can keep the hardware busy, since different stages are working on different pieces of data at the same time. The pipelining gives you the parallelism that the GPU has to get from batch size.

And that matters a lot in practice, especially for inference, where latency is important and you often don't have the luxury of waiting to accumulate a huge batch. It also matters for training very large models, where memory capacity limits how big your batch can be anyway. So the short version is: the GPU serializes in time and leans on batch to recover efficiency, while dataflow spreads the computation out in space and gets efficiency through pipelining, which frees you from depending so heavily on large batches.

r001.rationale: The response says GPU kernels run one after another, while the RDU runs different operators concurrently in a pipeline, parallelizing work across operators.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it is that on a GPU, the way you get efficiency is by batching. You take a layer, you load it onto the chip, and then you run a big batch of inputs through that layer to amortize the cost of loading the weights and to keep all of those SIMD lanes busy. Then you go to the next layer, and you do the same thing. So in effect, execution is serialized by layer, or by kernel. Each kernel runs to completion, writes its results back out to memory, and then the next kernel starts and reads those results back in. And the only reason that's acceptable is because the batch is large enough that the compute dominates the memory traffic. If you shrink the batch, say for latency-sensitive inference where you have one request at a time, the GPU becomes very inefficient, because now you're paying the full cost of moving weights and activations in and out of memory for a tiny amount of useful work.

On the RDU, the reconfigurable dataflow unit, the model is different. Instead of serializing the computation kernel by kernel, we map a whole sequence of layers, or the entire model if it fits, spatially onto the chip. So layer one is in one region of the chip, layer two is in another region, and so on, and the activations flow directly from one to the next through on-chip memory and the on-chip interconnect without ever going back out to off-chip memory. That's the dataflow part. What that means is that different layers are executing concurrently on different parts of the chip, pipelined, rather than one after another.

So the serialization that's fundamental to the GPU model goes away. You don't need a big batch to get efficiency, because you're not amortizing weight loads across a batch; you're keeping the weights resident and streaming the data through. You can run with batch size one and still keep the chip busy, because the parallelism comes from the spatial pipeline rather than from the width of the batch. And the bonus is that you also eliminate a lot of the memory bandwidth pressure, because the intermediate activations never leave the chip.

Now, if you do have a large batch, you can use it too. The two things compose. But the point is that on the RDU batching is an optimization you can choose, whereas on the GPU it's a requirement to get anywhere near peak performance. And that distinction becomes really important when you look at where the workloads are going, toward inference, toward low latency, toward models that are too big to fit comfortably into the batch-and-kernel paradigm.

r001.rationale: It says GPU execution is serialized layer by layer, while an RDU runs different layers concurrently in a spatial pipeline, removing that serialization.

astra-6.text:
The key question is what you’re serializing. On a GPU, you typically execute the model one operation at a time. You take a batch through one operation, write the intermediate results to memory, and then bring them back for the next operation. Batching lets you do more work at each step, but the operations are still sequenced in time.

On an RDU, we can lay out a sequence of operations spatially and stream data through them. As one part of the batch moves into the next operation, the following data can enter the previous one. So you get a pipeline, with different operations working concurrently, and you can keep intermediate results on chip. You still have dependencies, of course, but you’re exploiting parallelism across the operations as well as within them.

r001.rationale: The response says GPU operations are sequenced in time, while an RDU can run different operations concurrently in a pipeline, directly communicating that the RDU parallelizes this serialization.

sol-6.1.text:
The key question is how much of the computation has to be serialized. On a GPU, you typically execute a sequence of kernels. You do one operation across the batch, write the results back to memory, and then launch the next operation. Batching gives you more parallel work within each of those stages, but the stages still happen sequentially.

On an RDU, we can map a sequence of operations spatially onto the architecture and stream data between them. So while one part of the batch is going through a later stage, another part can be entering an earlier stage. You still have the dependencies inherent in the computation, but you can pipeline across them instead of executing each stage across the whole batch before moving on. That means you don’t have to depend as heavily on a large batch to keep the machine busy.

r001.rationale: The response says GPU stages happen sequentially, while an RDU can pipeline operations so different parts of the batch occupy different stages at once.
